confidence_note: Book not read. Atlassian details from an ASMP blog and a web search; 2005 start and 24-hour rule agree, but the 2005 version is described as a day and a half in one account. Old text's monthly day in 2006, dozens of products and Gmail/Maps claims dropped. No measured outcomes, so the story stays modest on results.
facts: Atlassian introduced FedEx Days in 2005; now called ShipIt Day.
The name borrows FedEx's promise to ship overnight; participants get 24 hours to originate, develop and deliver something.
One account says the 2005 version gave developers about a day and a half to build something out of the ordinary and show colleagues at the end.
Aims: break routines, try unfamiliar technology, tackle a small project, often with a coworker.
Format modeled on Google's 20 percent time.
Pink's autonomy covers what you do, when, how and with whom.
Companies report expanded skills, new collaborations and renewed excitement; no measured figures.
scene_details: a small project built with a coworker
tension: A company hands people a day with almost no rules except a deadline.
opening_idea: A day to build anything, one condition.

lessons.idea: Give a small piece of time with one fixed edge.
lessons.anchor: the 24-hour deadline with free choice of topic

reflect_final: If you had one day and a fixed hour to show the result, what would you choose to build, and with whom?

use_cases.move: Propose one day outside the roadmap with a show-and-tell at the end.
Let them pick the project and helper, with a showing at lunch.
Set a 24-hour clock and show a friend at the end.

pocket_idea: Atlassian fixed only the clock: 24 hours, any topic, then show it.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: Atlassian's FedEx Day fixed only the clock.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: 24 hours, anything, show it; origin 2005; Google 20 percent.
